title: How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: An NVIDIA tutorial shows how to use the KvikIO Python library on top of the cuFile API to read data straight from NVMe into GPU memory with GPUDirect Storage, and how to confirm the accelerated nvidia-fs path via cuFile statistics (a 1 GiB read split into 256 nvfs operations on an H100). The key point is that KvikIO and cuFile make separate path decisions, so reaching cuFile does not guarantee acceleration, and tuning task size and cufile.json settings shapes how requests are split.

themes.theme: Data movement as the AI bottleneck

insights.claim: Citing the 2025 Stanford AI Index, NVIDIA notes that compute for notable AI models has been doubling roughly every five months and LLM training dataset size roughly every eight months, making efficient storage-to-GPU data movement necessary to keep accelerators supplied.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: Storage I/O is becoming a gating factor for GPU utilization, which supports demand for GDS-capable storage vendors and NVMe.
insights.quote: compute for notable AI models has been doubling approximately every five months, while the size of datasets used to train LLMs has been doubling approximately every eight months.
insights.locator: GPU applications are processing ever-growing datasets

insights.claim: NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) creates a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory, avoiding staging through CPU memory and reducing CPU utilization, and is supported by many major storage vendors.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: GDS support is a competitive checkbox for AI storage vendors selling into NVIDIA GPU clusters.

insights.claim: NVIDIA notes that as of August 2025 nearly half of new AI projects on GitHub were built primarily in Python, while GDS's main application interface is the cuFile C API, a gap that the KvikIO Python and C++ library fills.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: Python-native wrappers are how NVIDIA extends low-level CUDA features to the mainstream AI developer base.
insights.locator: At the application layer, Python plays

insights.claim: KvikIO and cuFile make separate I/O path decisions: KvikIO chooses between calling cuFile and its own CPU-staged POSIX path, and cuFile then chooses between the accelerated nvidia-fs GDS path and its own CPU-staged compatibility path, so reaching cuFile alone does not confirm GDS acceleration.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: Deployments may silently fall back to CPU-staged I/O, so claimed GDS speedups need verification.
insights.quote: reaching the cuFile API confirms that KvikIO selected cuFile, but does not by itself confirm that the accelerated GDS path was activated.
insights.locator: How does NVIDIA KvikIO leverage GDS?

insights.claim: KvikIO defaults to AUTO compatibility mode, which tries cuFile and falls back to POSIX if cuFile is unavailable, and has a 16 KiB GDS threshold below which reads go straight to the POSIX path; both are controllable via KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE and KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: Default fallbacks keep code portable but can hide whether GPU-direct I/O is in use.
insights.locator: On the tutorial system, KvikIO reports

insights.claim: Setting CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and inspecting with gds_stats shows whether cuFile operations used the nvidia-fs path (nvfs counters) or the compatibility path (posix counters); forcing CUFILE_FORCE_COMPAT_MODE shifts operations to posix, and KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE=on bypasses cuFile entirely.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: Gives operators a concrete check for whether GPU storage acceleration is actually active in production.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's GDS tutorial ran on an x86_64 system with an NVIDIA H100, CUDA 13.3 and cuFile 1.18, reading from a local ext4 NVMe drive over a PIX link (at most one PCIe bridge) with IOMMU and ACS disabled to preserve PCIe peer-to-peer transfers.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: GDS requires specific PCIe topology and disabling IOMMU/ACS, a deployment friction that can limit adoption in security-sensitive environments.

insights.claim: With KvikIO's default 4 MiB task size, a 1 GiB read into a CuPy GPU buffer was split into 256 operations, and cuFile statistics showed n=256, nvfs=256 and posix=0, meaning every operation took the accelerated nvidia-fs path.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: Shows a verifiable end-to-end GPU-direct read is achievable from plain Python.

insights.claim: KvikIO first splits requests by KVIKIO_TASK_SIZE and schedules them with KVIKIO_NTHREADS, and cuFile can split each request again using cufile.json settings such as execution.parallel_io, max_io_threads, min_io_threshold_size_kb, max_request_parallelism and max_io_queue_depth.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: Two-level tuning knobs mean GDS performance depends heavily on configuration expertise.

insights.claim: With a 1 GiB KvikIO task size, cuFile splits the read into four 256 MiB pieces (capped by four workers and a max request parallelism of four), but because the CuPy buffer is unregistered, cuFile reads through registered GPU bounce buffers, configurable as slabs since GDS 1.17 and no larger than 16 MiB on the nvidia-fs path.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: Unregistered buffers add an extra GPU copy, so registering buffers is a lever for squeezing more I/O throughput.
insights.locator: A 1 GiB read, step by step

insights.claim: cuFile's 8 MiB min_io_threshold_size_kb target does not change a 1 GiB split but makes cuFile schedule a 16 MiB request as two 8 MiB pieces rather than four 4 MiB ones, and KvikIO must use a task size of at least 16 MiB for cuFile to receive that request intact.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: A tuning detail for I/O-bound GPU pipelines; it matters mainly to infrastructure engineers.
insights.locator: When the 8 MiB split target matters

insights.claim: KvikIO is part of NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries for data science (formerly RAPIDS) and grew out of GDS integration built for cuDF, where parallel cuFile reads accelerated Parquet and ORC ingestion; it has since been used in cuCIM digital pathology, the cuPhoton xDataReader, and GPU-accelerated Presto analytics.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoyle
insights.so_what: GPU-accelerated analytics (cuDF, Presto) extends NVIDIA's addressable market from AI training into data engineering, with storage I/O as an enabler.
insights.locator: KvikIO in NVIDIA CUDA-X for data science
